read: full (pp.1-12 and appendices A, B, C, E read; example solutions in appendices D and F skimmed)
venue_now: arXiv preprint only in the text (arXiv:2110.14168v2, 18 Nov 2021, p.1 stamp); no venue shown
what_it_is: A paper that introduces GSM8K, 8.5K grade-school maths word problems written by human contractors, each with a natural-language solution of 2 to 8 elementary arithmetic steps (pp.1-3), and that proposes training verifiers (outcome-supervised: labelled only by whether a sampled solution reaches the correct final answer) to rank 100 sampled solutions at test time (pp.5, 7-8). Performance is the solve rate of the final answer (p.5). Its main result is that a 6B verifier slightly outperforms a fine-tuned 175B model, about a 30x model-size gain (p.12). The dataset is static and was quality-checked by having workers re-solve every problem (p.15).
size: 8.5K problems: 7.5K train, 1K test as stated (p.3; GSM-Symbolic p.4 gives the released split as 7,473 / 1,319); models: GPT-3 3B, 6B, 12B, 175B fine-tuned (p.6, Fig. 2)
source_of_items: expert-written in the loose sense: written by paid contractors (Upwork, then Surge AI), who could start from seed questions generated by few-shot prompted GPT-3 175B (p.15)
has_gold_traces: partial: every problem has a human-written natural-language solution (pp.2-3) with calculator annotations added by hard-coded logic and a fine-tuned model (p.17); the solutions are training data, and nothing scores a model's steps against them
evaluation: final answer (single low-temperature sample checked for the correct final answer, p.5; test@N for N samples, p.7); the verifier itself is an outcome reward model (pp.5, 7)
human_validation: Items: after collection, workers re-solved all problems (never their own); disagreeing problems were repaired or discarded; a second agreement round on a smaller subset found 1.7% still disagree, taken as the estimated rate of breaking errors or ambiguities (p.15; 'less than 2 percent', p.3). Contractors received similarity-score feedback so as not to reuse templates (p.15). No validation of any evaluator is reported.
contamination_measures: none stated; problems were newly written rather than scraped (p.3), but the paper does not frame this as a contamination measure

engtrace_use.sentence: S-M1 (L155-161): 'In mathematics, benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom (Gulati et al., 2024), and GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability.'
engtrace_use.explanation: GSM8K consists of grade-school word problems solved by 2 to 8 elementary arithmetic steps, which 'a bright middle school student should be able to solve' (p.3). Its authors present it as probing 'informal reasoning ability' (p.2), with the main difficulty in 'properly interpreting a question and reasoning through the steps' (p.4). 'Abstract logical deduction' is a loose name for that, and GSM8K has no stability component: it is one fixed test split (p.3), and GSM-Symbolic is the work that adds instantiation variance. 'Rigorously' also overstates the check. The benchmark scores only whether the final answer is correct (p.5), and the paper itself notes that 'some solutions will reach the correct final answer using flawed reasoning, leading to false positives' (p.7). The gist holds: a mathematics benchmark at the easy end of a range, with no physical grounding. So the use is imprecise rather than misleading.

suggested_wording: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) poses 8.5K human-written grade-school word problems of two to eight arithmetic steps and scores only the final answer, although its authors note that sampled solutions can reach the correct answer through flawed reasoning.
facts_to_cite: 8.5K grade-school maths word problems written by human problem writers, split 7.5K train / 1K test (p.3)
Problems take 2 to 8 steps of elementary arithmetic (+, -, x, /) (p.3)
Each problem comes with a natural-language solution (pp.2-3)
Performance is judged by whether a single low-temperature sample reaches the correct final answer (p.5)
Verifiers are trained only on final-answer correctness, and 'some solutions will reach the correct final answer using flawed reasoning, leading to false positives' (p.7)
Fine-tuning a 6B model to output the answer without intermediate steps drops performance from 20.6% to 5.2% (p.7)
6B verification slightly outperforms a fine-tuned 175B model, roughly a 30x model-size gain (p.12)
Workers re-solved all problems; 1.7% still produced disagreements in a later check, the estimated rate of breaking errors (p.15)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-step quantitative word problems with a worked solution per problem (pp.2-3) and a deterministic final-answer check (p.5); its verifier work is the outcome-supervision baseline that process supervision answers (pp.5-9). Lacks: generated instances (static, human-written, p.3); step-level evaluation (final answer only, p.5); any engineering or physical content; expert validation of an evaluator (only answer agreement among workers re-solving items, p.15).
notes: The paper is as much a verifier paper as a benchmark paper: its verifiers are outcome reward models (labels from final-answer correctness only, p.7), and a token-level variant is described as a value function (p.9). That makes it a natural citation in the planned paragraph on process supervision, as the outcome-supervised baseline, with the p.7 false-positive remark as motivation for step-level checking. The stated 1K test split (p.3) is rounded; the released test set has 1,319 problems (GSM-Symbolic, p.4). No venue appears in the text.
